differentiability-s1.title: The graph of a function $g$ on $[-3, 4]$
differentiability-s1.text: The graph of $g$ is made of a line segment on $[-3, 0]$, part of the parabola $y = \frac{x^2}{2}$ on $[0, 2]$, and part of the curve $y = 1 + \sqrt[3]{x - 3}$ on $(2, 4]$.

plot.label: Graph of g: a line falling from (-3, 3) to (0, 0), a parabola rising from (0, 0) to a closed dot at (2, 2), then an open dot at (2, 0) where a cube-root curve begins, rising steeply through (3, 1) to (4, 2)

differentiability-s2.title: A piecewise function that joins smoothly

plot.label: Graph of p: the parabola y = x squared for x up to 1, joined at (1, 1) by the line y = 2x minus 1 for x greater than 1

items.q: At which values of $x$ in the open interval $(-3, 4)$ is $g$ not differentiable? Select every one.

why.correct: A corner at $x = 0$, a jump at $x = 2$ and a vertical tangent at $x = 3$. Everywhere else the graph is smooth.
options: The graph is a straight line here, with slope $-1$.
A corner: slope $-1$ on the left, 0 on the right.
The parabola is smooth here, with slope 1.
A jump: $g$ is not continuous at 2, so it is not differentiable there.
The curve is vertical at $(3, 1)$: the difference quotients grow without bound.
The curve is smooth here, with a finite slope.
It is neither continuous nor differentiable.
It is continuous but not differentiable.
It is differentiable at 2 but not continuous at 2.
It is both continuous and differentiable.

why.correct: $\lim_{x \to 2^-} g(x) = 2$ and $\lim_{x \to 2^+} g(x) = 0$, so $g$ is not continuous at 2, and a function that is not continuous cannot be differentiable.
options: A jump breaks continuity, and with it differentiability.
The one-sided limits are 2 and 0, so $g$ is not continuous at 2.
Differentiable implies continuous, so this combination is impossible.
There is a jump at $x = 2$.
The tangent line at $(3, 1)$ is vertical: the slopes grow without bound.
$g(3)$ is not defined, so there is no point to take a slope at.
$g$ is not continuous at $x = 3$.
The graph has a corner at $x = 3$, with two different finite slopes.

why.correct: Near $x = 3$ the curve $1 + \sqrt[3]{x - 3}$ is steeper and steeper; the slopes have no finite limit.
options: A vertical tangent line has no finite slope.
$g(3) = 1$; the point is on the graph.
The curve passes through $(3, 1)$ without a break, so $g$ is continuous there.
Both sides become infinitely steep in the same direction; there are no two finite slopes.

items.q: Which statement best explains why $g$ is not differentiable at $x = 0$?
options: $g$ is continuous at 0, but the difference quotient approaches $-1$ from the left and 0 from the right.
$g$ is not continuous at 0, because two different formulas meet there.
$g(0) = 0$, and a function has no derivative where its value is 0.
The graph is level at $x = 0$, so $g'(0)$ does not exist.

why.correct: On the left the graph is the line $y = -x$ (slope $-1$); on the right the parabola $\frac{x^2}{2}$ has slope $x$, which is 0 at $x = 0$. Two different one-sided slopes make a corner.
options: Continuous, but the one-sided slopes differ: a corner.
Both formulas give 0 at $x = 0$, so $g$ is continuous; a change of formula alone breaks nothing.
A function can be 0 and still have a derivative; $x^2$ does at $x = 0$.
A level tangent line would mean $g'(0) = 0$, which exists; here no single tangent line exists.
Yes: both pieces approach 1 and $p(1) = 1$.
No: $p$ is defined by two different formulas.
Yes, because the graph has no sharp point there.
The one-sided limits and the value agree.
Two formulas can still join without a break.
Continuity depends on the limits and the value, not on whether the graph is smooth.
It does not exist, because $p$ changes formula at $x = 1$.

why.correct: From the left, $x^2$ has slope $2x = 2$ at $x = 1$; from the right, the line $2x - 1$ has slope 2. Equal one-sided slopes and continuity give $p'(1) = 2$.
options: The left slope 2 matches the right slope 2.
That is $p(1)$, the height, not the slope.
A change of formula does not by itself prevent a derivative; the slopes here match.
That adds the two one-sided slopes; they must be equal, and then $p'(1)$ is their common value.

items.q: Suppose the second piece of $p$ is changed to $3x - 2$ for $x > 1$. Which is true at $x = 1$?
options: $p$ is continuous but not differentiable.
$p$ is differentiable, with $p'(1) = 3$.
$p$ is neither continuous nor differentiable.
$p$ is differentiable, with $p'(1) = 2.5$.

why.correct: $3(1) - 2 = 1$, so the pieces still meet: continuous. But the slopes are 2 on the left and 3 on the right, a corner.
options: The pieces meet, but the slopes 2 and 3 differ.
The slope is 3 only on the right; on the left it is 2.
Both pieces give 1 at $x = 1$, so there is no break.
Averaging two one-sided slopes does not make a derivative; they must be equal.

items.q: Suppose instead the second piece of $p$ is changed to $2x + 1$ for $x > 1$. Which is true at $x = 1$?
options: $p$ is not continuous, so it is not differentiable.
$p$ is differentiable, because both pieces have slope 2.
$p$ is continuous but not differentiable.
$p$ is continuous and differentiable.

why.correct: From the right $2x + 1 \to 3$, but $p(1) = 1$: a jump. A function that is not continuous at a point has no derivative there.
options: The jump from 1 to 3 breaks continuity, and differentiability needs continuity.
Equal slopes on the two sides are not enough; the pieces must also meet.
The right-hand limit is 3 and $p(1) = 1$, so $p$ is not continuous.
There is a jump at $x = 1$.

items.q: Which statement is true for every function $f$?
options: If $f$ is differentiable at $a$, then $f$ is continuous at $a$.
If $f$ is continuous at $a$, then $f$ is differentiable at $a$.
If $f$ is not differentiable at $a$, then $f$ is not continuous at $a$.
If $f(a)$ is defined, then $f$ is differentiable at $a$.
The theorem: a derivative at $a$ forces continuity at $a$.
The converse is false: $|x|$ is continuous at 0 but not differentiable there.
False: $|x|$ is not differentiable at 0 yet is continuous there.
A value at $a$ does not even guarantee continuity, let alone a derivative.

items.q: A function $f$ is continuous at $x = a$. What can you conclude about $f'(a)$?
options: $f'(a)$ may or may not exist.
$f'(a)$ exists, because continuity guarantees a slope.
$f'(a)$ does not exist.

why.correct: Continuity is necessary for a derivative but not sufficient: $x^2$ (differentiable at 0) and $|x|$ (not differentiable at 0) are both continuous at 0.
options: Continuity alone does not decide it.
A corner, cusp or vertical tangent can be continuous with no derivative.
Many continuous functions, such as $x^2$, do have derivatives.
A slope and a height are different quantities.
$f$ is continuous but not differentiable.
$f$ is differentiable, with $f'(3) = 0$.
$f$ is neither continuous nor differentiable.
$f$ is differentiable, with $f'(3) = 1$.

why.correct: The graph is a V with its point at $(3, 0)$: no break, but slope $-1$ on the left and 1 on the right.
options: A corner: continuous, one-sided slopes $-1$ and 1.
The lowest point is a corner, not a smooth bottom with a level tangent line.
Both sides approach $f(3) = 0$, so $f$ is continuous.
The slope is 1 only to the right of 3.

items.q: Let $f(x) = x^{2/3}$. Which describes the graph of $f$ at $x = 0$?
options: A cusp: $f$ is continuous, and the slopes become infinitely steep in opposite directions.
A corner: $f$ is continuous, and the slopes are $-1$ on the left and 1 on the right.
A jump: $f$ is not continuous at 0.
A smooth bottom: $f'(0) = 0$.

why.correct: The difference quotient $\frac{h^{2/3}}{h} = \frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{h}}$ goes to $-\infty$ from the left and $+\infty$ from the right.
options: Infinite slopes of opposite signs make a cusp.
The slopes are not finite numbers here; they grow without bound.
$h^{2/3} \to 0 = f(0)$ from both sides, so $f$ is continuous.
The quotient $\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{h}}$ does not approach 0; it grows without bound.
$f$ is continuous, but not differentiable, because the tangent line is vertical.
$f$ is differentiable, because the graph has no corner.
$f$ is not continuous, because $\sqrt[3]{0} = 0$.
$f$ is differentiable, with $f'(0) = 0$.

why.correct: $\frac{\sqrt[3]{h} - 0}{h} = \frac{1}{h^{2/3}} \to +\infty$ from both sides: the graph passes through the origin with a vertical tangent line.
options: A vertical tangent line means an infinite slope: no derivative.
No corner is not enough; the slope here is infinite.
A value of 0 has nothing to do with continuity; $\sqrt[3]{x}$ is continuous everywhere.
The graph is as steep as possible at 0, not level.

items.q: A student writes: "$f$ is not differentiable at $x = 2$, so $f$ is not continuous at $x = 2$." Which response is correct?
options: The reasoning is wrong: $f(x) = |x - 2|$ is continuous at 2 but not differentiable there.
The reasoning is right: differentiability and continuity mean the same thing.
The reasoning is right: it is the theorem that differentiable functions are continuous.
The reasoning is wrong: a function that is not differentiable is continuous.

why.correct: The theorem runs one way: differentiable implies continuous. Its converse, and the student's statement, can fail.
options: One counterexample shows the claim is false.
They differ: corners, cusps and vertical tangents are continuous points with no derivative.
The student reversed the theorem; "not differentiable" says nothing about continuity.
A jump is not differentiable and not continuous either; no conclusion either way.

items.q: For a continuous function $f$, $\lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{f(5 + h) - f(5)}{h} = 2$ and $\lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{f(5 + h) - f(5)}{h} = -1$. What is $f'(5)$?
options: It does not exist.
$\frac{1}{2}$, the average of the one-sided limits

why.correct: The two-sided limit exists only when the one-sided limits are equal. Here they differ, so the graph has a corner at $x = 5$.
options: Different one-sided limits: no two-sided limit.
Averaging the one-sided slopes does not give a derivative.
That is only the slope from the left.
That is only the slope from the right.

items.q: Let $f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 & x \le 2 \\ mx + b & x > 2 \end{cases}$, where $m$ and $b$ are constants. If $f$ is differentiable at $x = 2$, what is $b$?

mistakes.why: That is $m$, the slope: $m$ must match the slope of $x^2$ at 2, which is $2(2) = 4$. Then use continuity, $2m + b = 4$, to find $b$.
The slope of $x^2$ at $x = 2$ is $2x = 4$, not 2. With $m = 4$, continuity gives $8 + b = 4$.

why.correct: Differentiable at 2 means continuous at 2 and equal one-sided slopes. Slopes: $m = 2(2) = 4$. Continuity: $2m + b = 2^2$, so $8 + b = 4$ and $b = -4$.
